Pacific halibut (Hippoglossus stenolepis) embryos develop within transparent, yolk-laden pelagic eggs that drift in the water column for a period after spawning. When incubation occurs at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time since hatch at birth is approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days], a relatively rapid eclosion compared to many other flatfishes that spawn in colder waters. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, still in a lecithotrophic state, measures only a few millimeters in length and relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves. The wet weight at birth is roughly 0.02 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.02 grams], a value derived from the small egg diameter of 3.4 mm. This initial mass is remarkably low for a species that will eventually attain an enormous body size, highlighting the extreme contrast between the vulnerable early larval stage and the massive adult form that develops after many years of growth. The larval period is characterized by rapid morphological changes as the fish progresses through the preflexion and flexion stages, feeding actively on copepod nauplii and other small zooplankton in the pelagic environment.

During the early life stages, which occur in the cold waters of the Bering Sea and the Gulf of Alaska, larval development proceeds at a thermal regime of 5 °C [T = 5 °C]. Under these conditions, the time since hatch at metamorphosis, when the larvae undergo dramatic body plan reorganisation and settle to the benthos, is approximately 183 days from hatch [tj = approximately 183 da at a temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C]ys from hatch]. This extended larval duration reflects the slow developmental rates typical of high-latitude marine fishes and allows the larvae to grow sufficiently before the demanding transition to a benthic existence. The larval-juvenile transition involves the migration of one eye to the opposite side of the head, a profound morphological transformation that characterizes all pleuronectiform flatfishes. During this period, the growing juveniles begin to exploit a diet of small crustaceans and eventually small fish, accumulating the energy reserves necessary for continued somatic growth. The timing of this habitat shift is critical, as it coincides with the availability of suitable benthic prey and protects the young fish from the intense predation pressure faced by pelagic larvae.

Reproductive output in Pacific halibut is substantial, with females producing a large number of eggs during each spawning event in the cold waters typically found at 5 °C [T = 5 °C]. Observations indicate that the maximum reproductive rate reaches approximately 5,479 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 5,479 eggs per year], with females laying approximately 2 million eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2 million eggs per spawning event] and a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = single spawning event each year], a fecundity that is among the highest recorded for any marine fish. This enormous egg production is an adaptive response to the extremely high mortality rates experienced during the pelagic larval phase, where only a tiny fraction of offspring survive to metamorphosis. The eggs themselves are relatively small, approximately 3.4 mm in diameter, and are spawned in deep water where they float to the surface. The trade-off between egg size and fecundity is evident here, with the species investing in a high quantity of relatively small eggs rather than a smaller number of larger, more energy-rich oocytes. This strategy is common among broadcast-spawning marine teleosts that rely on the vast planktonic food web to support the early feeding stages.

As Pacific halibut mature, they undergo a prolonged period of somatic growth that eventually results in an extraordinary maximum size. The ultimate total length recorded for this species is 267 centimeters [Li = 267 centimeters], making it one of the largest flatfishes in the world. Correspondingly, the asymptotic wet weight attained by adult individuals reaches 363,000 grams [Wwi = 363,000 grams], a body mass that places the species at the apex of the benthic fish community in the North Pacific. This extreme size is achieved through a slow, steady growth trajectory that continues over many decades. At the cold temperatures typical of their habitat, approximately 5 °C [T = 5 °C], the maximum lifespan of Pacific halibut has been estimated at around 55 years [am = around 55 years], though some of the very largest individuals may be even older. The combination of a long lifespan and indeterminate growth allows females to produce ever-larger clutches as they age, contributing disproportionately to the population's reproductive output. Old, large females are particularly valuable to the fishery and to the species' population dynamics because they release more eggs and potentially produce larvae with higher survival rates.

Puberty in female Pacific halibut occurs after an extended juvenile period, reflecting the slow pace of life history characteristic of this long-lived, cold-water species. At a temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C], the time since birth at puberty for females is approximately 12 years since birth [tp = approximately 12 years since birth], a delayed maturation that allows the fish to accumulate sufficient body size and energy reserves before initiating the energetically costly process of gamete production. This age at sexual maturity is consistent with the species' position as a top predator in a high-latitude, relatively low-productivity ecosystem. The onset of gonadal activity marks a major life-history transition, after which individuals allocate a significant portion of their annual energy budget to vitellogenesis and spermiation. Males typically mature at a slightly younger age and smaller size than females, a pattern common among fishes with indeterminate growth and sexual size dimorphism. The long period of pre-pubertal growth allows the species to capitalize on its indeterminate growth strategy, ensuring that by the time reproduction begins, individuals are large enough to produce a substantial number of offspring and to survive the rigors of repeated spawning migrations.
